comments.text: Dispatch to the music initialization routine at $1C78. The title calls this with A=0.
Dispatch to $20C1. Callers put a sound effect number in A.
Dispatch to $1D5C, which replaces the sound mode byte with $20. The normal IRQ dispatcher then follows its idle path.
Inspect mode bits at $1305. Bit 7 selects the music path, bit 6 selects the effects path when bit 7 is clear, and clearing both gates all three SID voices off.
Embedded driver credit beginning MUSIC AND CODE (C) MARK TAIT.
Decrement the shared tempo counter, and on rollover process each due voice's stream. $FE stops the music and $FF restarts the selected tune. Other high-bit bytes dispatch to commands through $1766.
Convert a track byte through the per-voice offset and pitch table. Read its duration, advance the track pointer and retrigger the SID voice if the voice's control flags permit.
Step the master fade when active, then process the per-voice note gate and modulation counters.
Skip inactive voices; active voices enter the pitch and waveform updates. The gate-off test just above can also reach this path.
Music initialization sets bit 7. Queueing a sound effect sets bit 6, and the idle dispatcher at $1009 tests these bits in that order.
Register offsets 0, 7 and 14 used to address the three seven-register SID voice groups.
Song index retained by $1C79. A track end marker of $FF restarts this selection.
Tempo divisor installed by $1CC4 and copied into the shared countdown on rollover at $1053.
The three low bytes of the current per-voice stream pointers. $105F reads a low byte before decoding the next sound event.
The high bytes paired with the current stream pointer lows at $1313. $10EE stores the updated high byte.
Initial SID control values for the three music voices, loaded from the tune parameters.
Per-voice ticks remaining before the parser reads another event for that voice. The initializer staggers these to 1, 2 and 3.
Shared sub-tick counter. On zero, reload it from $130A and step the track counters.
Little-endian SID frequency words indexed by twice the note number. The first word is zero. The effect player reads the low and high parts at $2098 and $209E.
High byte of the first pitch word, the base of the second indexed read in the effects player.
Six offsets into the tune's six-byte voice pointer set. $1C7C chooses the source record with the incoming song number.
Six offsets into the tune records at $155D. Values advance by 18 bytes per song.
Six offsets into $153F. The initializer selects a ten-byte record with this table.
Song parameters, each consisting of AD and SR for each voice, a tempo reload byte, and three voice control values. $1C9D begins the copy.
Eighteen bytes per tune copied into the player working data at $138D by $1CE1.
Three six-byte track-pointer sets precede the pointer-advance code here: lows for voices 1–3 followed by highs for voices 1–3.
Increment the 16-bit bytecode pointer in $A7/$A8. If the low byte wraps, increment the high byte.
Advance the track pointer by Y plus one so command handlers skip the opcode and all the operands read so far.
Set the fade-active byte and load the current and reload fade intervals from the command operand.
Enable the early gate-off check for this voice and store the remaining-note-tick threshold from the following track byte.
Clear the current voice's early gate-off enable and fetch the next track event.
Select cached SID control $42 for this voice, then advance one byte.
Select cached SID control $50 for this voice, then advance one byte.
Select cached SID control $40 for this voice, then advance one byte.
Select cached SID control $46 for this voice, then advance one byte.
Clear this voice's cached control value, then advance one byte.
Read two parameter bytes into $138D,X and $13C4,X, enable the mode at $13C1,X and clear the alternate mode at $1349,X.
Clear the per-voice values at $13C1 and $13C4 and continue with the next stream command.
Select the alternate modulation mode at $1349,X. Store the three following parameters and save half of the last byte in $1355,X.
Clear the voice setting at $1349,X and resume track decoding.
Read the repeat counter and save the pointer to the first event after the command and operand.
Decrement the saved repeat counter. If nonzero, reload the saved track pointer before decoding the next event.
Read two track operands into the voice slots at $1390 and $1393, which are copied to $13AF and $13AC when the note retriggers.
Read repeat count, pitch offset and target pointer. Save the following track address, then decode the phrase at the supplied pointer.
Decrement the phrase counter. Jump back to the phrase start while nonzero, then restore the return pointer and clear the pitch offset.
Set the flag consulted at $11B6 for this voice and advance to the following event.
Clear the flag consulted by the active voice at $11B6.
Enable the voice mode at $1340 and read two parameters. Store the first in $1358 and $135B, and the second in $1346.
Clear the mode flag at $1340 for the selected voice and advance one byte.
Set the flag at $13A9 which causes $1101 to skip the SID note retrigger.
Clear the flag tested at $10FE and resume track decoding.
Handler pointers for the high-bit command bytes $80–$B4. $1089 masks the high bit and doubles the remainder to select a word. The first eleven entries point back to the table.
Initial phrase storage before the title's track entries. The title stream beginning at $1853 uses a $95 command with target $17D0, one repeat and a pitch offset of $0C.
First track pointer loaded for tune zero. The opening uses a timed zero pitch, command $B3 and a phrase call through $95.
Second track pointer for tune zero. Set the gate threshold then call the phrase at $185F before the $FF marker.
Third track for tune zero. Uses the $B3 gate setting and $8E modulation setup ahead of the opening pitched note events.
First voice of tune one. The opening phrase target is $1AEE and the terminating command is $FE.
Second voice of tune one. Its $95 command calls the phrase at $1B2C without a pitch offset.
Third voice of tune one. Its $95 call transposes the phrase at $1B77 by $24 before stopping.
First track entry for tune two, calling the phrase at $1BC5 and transposing the timed pitches by $0C.
Second track entry for tune two, using pitch offset $18 in the phrase call to $1BF3.
Third track entry for tune two, with a call to phrase $1C2A, followed by $FE.
Select a tune from A, load the three track pointers, timing, AD/SR and voice settings, reset playback state and turn on music mode in $1305.
Replace the music mode with $20 so both active mode tests at $1009 are clear on the next tick.
One byte per effects slot. Queueing sets it and the sequencer clears it when the pitch stream reaches $FF.
One cursor per effects slot, reset by $20FA and incremented after each pitch and control step.
Low bytes of the current effects note-stream pointers, one per voice.
Effect note-stream pointer high bytes, paired with $1D68.
Waveform and gate sequence pointer low bytes for the three effects slots.
High bytes paired with $1D6E. The player writes from this sequence to SID control using the pitch cursor.
Effect 0 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $47, $42, $46.
Effect 0 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $11.
Effect 1 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $42, $42, $42.
Effect 1 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 2 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $18, $24, $1F.
Effect 2 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Effect 3 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $32, $49, $26.
Effect 3 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $11.
Effect 4 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $33, $40, $20.
Effect 4 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $11.
Effect 5 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $2F, $40, $2D.
Effect 5 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Effect 6 pitch sequence, 32 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $17, $46, $3C.
Effect 6 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 7 pitch sequence, 35 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $17, $46, $3C.
Effect 7 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 8 pitch sequence, 16 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $3A, $39, $3A.
Effect 8 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 9 pitch sequence, 17 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $30, $30, $30.
Effect 9 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Effect 10 pitch sequence, 16 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $3C, $3A, $38.
Effect 10 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 11 pitch sequence, 3 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $30, $2F, $32.
Effect 11 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $21.
Effect 12 pitch sequence, 32 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $3A, $3B, $3C.
Effect 12 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $11.
Effect 13 pitch sequence, 40 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $30, $3C, $2C.
Effect 13 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Effect 14 pitch sequence, 8 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $3C, $30, $37.
Effect 14 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Effect 15 pitch sequence, 7 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $20, $21, $22.
Effect 15 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $21.
Effect 16 pitch sequence, 4 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $18, $18, $18.
Effect 16 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $21.
Effect 17 pitch sequence, 30 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $50, $4E, $4C.
Effect 17 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $81.
Effect 18 pitch sequence, 18 ticks before the $FF terminator. The first three pitch bytes are $0C, $10, $13.
Effect 18 control sequence read in parallel with the pitch bytes. The first control is $41.
Attack and decay register byte for each effect number, selected by $2107.
Sustain and release register byte for each effect number, selected by $210D.
Four bytes per effect: the little-endian pitch-sequence pointer and control-sequence pointer. $20D7 reads the selected record from A times four.
Walk the three effects slots. For each active slot, use the next note as a SID frequency lookup and write its matching waveform and gate. Pitch value $FF clears the slot.
Choose slot 0 if free, then slot 1 if free, otherwise use slot 2. Install A's two sequence pointers and configure the voice envelope, pulse width and starting control before entering effects mode.
Expand the serial stream into descending RAM addresses. The literal store is at $234B and the back-reference copy at $239F.
Set device 8 and open the filename already supplied by SETNAM. Make the drive talk so the next routine can read its compressed bytes.
Fetch five bytes into $FB-$FF through the KERNAL serial input routine, clear $A9, then bank out ROM and I/O and jump to $2300.
Temporarily expose KERNAL and I/O, update the input-byte countdown in $FE/$FF and read a serial byte. Return with RAM visible for the depacker stores.
Preserve the banking byte and border colour, read and expand a named file through the KERNAL serial routines, untalk after end of input and restore the port and border.
The cave lookup maps each character code to a contact class. $A64F indexes it after fetching the map byte. The cave-specific probes at $93C3, $940D and $943B also use it.
Contact classifications for catacombs tile IDs. Room setup patches $A650/$A651 to address this page for stage index one.
Contact classifications for airship tile IDs. Stage index two patches the map probe at $A64F to this page.
A page indexed by cave tile number, copied to colour lookup RAM at $3000 when the caves are active. The palette selector is zero.
Source for the catacombs' character-to-colour lookup. Selector one chooses this page from $B1B9.
The third page used by $B7C0 for the airship lookup. The temple path instead fills the lookup with $0B.
Prepared character codes for the logo. The title copies offsets 1–240 into the upper title screen from $042F, with colour 7.
The foreground sets this flag to 1 and waits at $7FB5. The gameplay IRQ clears it at $829A after servicing its pending work. The title IRQ clears it at $9974.
Cached value for the VIC memory-pointer register. The field IRQ can flip bit 5 to exchange the buffers at $0400 and $0C00. IRQ writes use this byte at $823A and $8271.
Low byte of horizontal scroll in pixels. The map renderer converts this and $7A2F to a tile column.
High byte of horizontal scroll in pixels, combined with $7A2E at $8873.
Low byte of vertical scroll in pixels. The map renderer combines this and $7A31 to choose the first map row.
High byte of vertical scroll in pixels, shifted into the map row index at $888B.
During gameplay, the lower-screen interrupt translates the low five active-low port 2 bits through $7A8D and stores the result here. The title uses this byte to hold its fire-bit test.
The first stage has a separate load for the train. $8F1B sets this flag on completion of the caves. $B814 reads it when the stage index is zero.
Low byte of the player world-space X coordinate, updated by $A37B and $A3FD. The map probe adds its requested horizontal offset before dividing by eight.
High byte of the player world-space X coordinate, propagated with carry or borrow by the horizontal movement routines.
Low byte of the player world-space Y coordinate. The map probe adds a vertical offset to it before choosing a map row.
High byte of the player world-space Y coordinate, read at $A5C7 while converting a probe point to a tile row.
Low-byte cave light accumulator at $8BA4. It wraps to advance the visible dimming stage and is reset on the palette-restoring pickup path.
Number of cave light timer carries since reset. Used to choose the palette replacement at $8BB2 and the displayed torch sprite at $8C18.
Sixteen coordinate bytes read in pairs by the panel IRQ. It copies them into $D000–$D00F.
Eight pointer bytes copied into the bank-3 sprite pointer slots by the panel IRQ. The cave torch and catacombs bolt logic update entries here.
Eight colours loaded into $D027–$D02E for the panel sprites.
Zero-based selection for caves/train, catacombs, airship and temple. $8F26 advances it when leaving the train or a later stage.
Clear the selected stage and loader cache, then initialize interrupts and hand off to the title setup via $976E.
Restore the gameplay interrupt and display settings, request room zero through $AC56 and initialize the stage before entering the foreground update loop at $7E68.
Wait for the raster task through the flag at $7E71, then run foreground game updates. Exits into a transition when $7F3C becomes nonzero.
Service the pending player animation change through $9635 when $7A8B is set, then set the raster mailbox at $7A29 and wait for the IRQ to clear it.
Blank the display, configure the VIC raster IRQ, select the title or play vector from the operand at $806F, and bank the KERNAL out before reenabling interrupts.
The vector set by $808D/$8092 points to this single RTI.
Briefly change the display mode at the raster split, then select screen $C000 and glyphs $C800 in VIC bank 3. Stage the panel sprite pointers, read port 2, tick music and schedule $81CF at line $F5.
Restore the field display and VIC bank 0, apply scroll and buffer selection from the game state, update colours or sprites, then schedule $809C at line $A6.
Choose the active screen page from $7A2B and patch the absolute-indexed sources in the unrolled colour copy. Use each character code as a lookup into the $3000 palette for colour RAM.
Burn time in an eight-pass outer loop with a 255-decrement inner loop, then return.

X supplies the destination screen page. Patch fifteen map row readers using the low and high pointer tables at $3400/$3500, then copy a viewport slice of character codes into the selected screen buffer.
Convert the unsigned 16-bit value in $FE/$FF to six digit codes at $7B34-$7B39 by repeated subtraction of decimal place values.
Fill six panel cells at $C379–$C37E with $D5 and set the active cell index to six.
Advance the current health cell's glyph once for each tick in A. Reaching $DD replaces that cell and moves to the preceding one. Exhausting the last cell calls $A2CF.
Add A to the 16-bit score at $7B30. Generate six digits and map them to status-panel glyphs at $C351.
Return the two's-complement magnitude of the signed byte in A. A nonnegative input returns immediately.
Negate the 16-bit value at $FE/$FF if its high byte has bit 7 set.
Nine sprite pointer values from $17 down to $10. $8B59 selects one from the bolt timer and writes it to the panel pointer table.
Add five to the lightning timer. On rollover advance the eight-state phase. Phase seven writes the bolt characters through the stage's pointer table and sets the background to colour 7.
Select different timer or hazard paths for the temple, airship, catacombs and train. The cave path advances the light timer and eventually remaps palette colours.
Advance a modulo-four counter and add two to the cave timer on three phases or one on phase zero. A timer carry advances the dimming stage.
Current colour codes to replace on selected dimming stages. A zero entry skips the palette rewrite.
Replacement colour for each dimming stage. $8BC3 reads this after the old colour test is selected.
Add the timer increment and, on carry, advance the dimming-stage index. Patch four parallel lookups to replace the stage's selected colour through $3000–$30FF.
Self-modified immediate byte of the first CMP in the dimming loop. $8BB7 installs the selected old colour here when the timer rolls over.
Self-modified immediate byte of the first LDA in the dimming loop. $8BC6 installs the selected replacement colour.
Select a 32-byte block by shifting A left five places. Copy 14 tile IDs to each of the two adjacent rows beginning at $664A and $674A.
Replacement tiles arranged in 32-byte groups. Each group starts with two 14-byte rows; $8D39 and $8D3F read their values separately and write them into the map.
First group's second row, the base address used for the second read at $8D3F. Each variant adds a 32-byte offset to this base.
Single RTS byte immediately after the preceding routine's return, before the next entry at $8EB4.
Switch from the cave subsection to the train first. After the train or a later stage, clear the subsection flag and advance the main stage index. Reenter setup at $7DD6.
Count X down through an entire byte range, then decrement Y and repeat while its sign bit stays clear.
Convert the player's world X into six panel glyphs at $C351 and world Y into a second six-glyph field at $C379. The caller of this path remains open.
A selects an eight-byte pattern at $CEE8. Copy each byte twice into $CF80, producing a vertically doubled 16-byte image.
Bank in the RAM beneath ROM and I/O with $01=$34. Select four component patterns through animation tables at $9696, $9702, $96CC and $9738. Copy or mirror each through $9C82, then restore $01=$35.
Set up the title-screen IRQ and VIC bank, convert the high score, copy six pages of title glyphs from $BB48 to $0800, draw the logo and start title music.
Synchronize with the IRQ, advance the attract-page timing and sample joystick port 2. Fire reaches the game-start path through $98C0.
Tick the driver except on the skipped timing slots, clear the foreground raster mailbox and keep the title IRQ on raster line zero.

Clear the message area, choose a stream using $9849 and consume its row records. Zero skips a row, a positive byte starts a row at that column and the following byte gives the colour. A negative row marker terminates the page and $FF ends a row's text.
Mask each message byte to six bits. Codes below $30 add $7C and codes from $30 add $3C, then write that glyph and the row colour to the output.
Twelve source bytes for the first subtitle row including its space padding. $980F converts it into the loaded title font's glyph numbers.
Source text for LAST CRUSADE. The title setup writes the converted glyphs at $0500.
Copyright, high-score digits and fire prompt in the row format that starts with column and colour, then text and a row terminator.
First credits stream selected by the second entry of $998A/$998E. The row commands position and colour the programmer, graphics, music and coordination credits.
Attract-text stream containing the message that Indy has rescued his father.
Row records selected by the fourth entry of $998A/$998E, containing the lives and continue display.

A selects a destination sprite layer, X and Y supply source address high and low. Patch the absolute load/store operands. Copy 64 bytes directly or use the reversal lookup and destination-byte permutation in the flipped path.
Four little-endian sprite destinations for the first bank of working player layers. Indexed by twice the layer number when the bank flag is clear.
Four little-endian sprite destinations used by the alternate working player layer buffer.
Save facing and animation state, then route on the action-state byte at $7B9A. State zero probes the map around the player and tests for new joystick actions.
Probe map classifications around the player at offsets $0C/$16, $04/$16 and $14/$16. Class 3 in these probes applies damage ticks before continuing to the support test.
Probe map classification at offset $0C/$26. Class $0C sets $7AAF, class zero goes to the unsupported path, and class 3 calls $A2CF.
An RTS follows the tail jump at $A338 and precedes the action branch target at $A33C.
Add A to world X and field-relative X. Past the right field threshold, transfer the increment to the camera unless the horizontal scroll limit is already reached.
Subtract A from world X and field-relative X. Crossing the left threshold can subtract the same amount from horizontal scroll while the camera has room to move.
Begin the upward motion path by subtracting A from the player's two-byte world Y.
Add A to world Y and field-relative Y, then transfer the increment to the camera when the lower field threshold and scroll limit permit it.

Take a horizontal offset in A and vertical offset in Y, convert the resulting world-space point into a tile coordinate and fetch the corresponding map character through $3400/$3500. Train and temple have specific return paths.
Compare the saved horizontal offset with $10. For smaller offsets decrement the 16-bit map pointer before fetching the next tile. The entry path into this block remains open.
Read the class byte for the tile in Y. The selected stage patches the operand so each loaded charset can give the same glyph index different contact semantics.
Read the original map column from the patched LDY operand. Clear this cell and its neighbour in two successive map rows before dispatching the contact reward.
Add 25 to the score, reset the two cave light counters and reinstall the stage palette.
Preserve the room index across disk loading, ensure the required asset set is resident, and initialize room state from the stage descriptor table through $B1D0.
Write 256 split row pointers from a base of $3600 into $3400 and $3500. Add the stage stride from $B19D and $B1A1 between adjacent pointers.
Use a stage-selected glyph to fill the shared playfield rows at $0400 and $0C00 and initialize colour RAM before drawing the room.
Set the room flags and player defaults, clear pending actions and build both sprite buffers. Initialize the display and per-room counters before entering play.

Stage-indexed records used by $AF00. The first byte is the tile ID. The pointer bytes at record offsets two and three give a target with a fixed $0A00 bias. Zero as the first byte terminates the sequence.
Three high bytes used to patch the contact table operand at $A651. They select $3100, $3200 and $3300.
Low bytes paired with $B197. The three pages are aligned at offset zero.
Low bytes of the map row stride for the four main stage indices. The catacombs use 150 bytes per row and the other indices use 256.
High bytes of the map row stride, paired with $B19D by the pointer-building loop at $AD03.
Source high bytes used by $B7DC when copying a stage's character-to-colour table. The train is the fifth selector.
Low bytes paired with $B1B9. Adding $80 gives the base of the second half of the source table.
Byte offsets into the working room descriptor page at $2700, in steps of 20. Indexed by the room selector at $ACA5.
Four little-endian pointers to the per-stage room descriptor collections. $AC8A selects one using twice the stage index.

Nine 20-byte records for the first stage. In each record, the first four little-endian values supply player world X/Y and camera scroll X/Y. Offsets $08–$0A initialize field-relative position and $12 selects the subsection.
Five 20-byte room records addressed by the stage-index-one pointer in $B1D0. Room setup uses the same record stride as the first stage.
Five 20-byte room descriptors for stage index two. The initial record starts with world X=$01E5 and Y=$002F.
Five 20-byte room descriptors for stage index three. The first record starts at X=0, Y=$003E with initial horizontal and vertical camera offsets of zero and six.
Start of the colour lookup copied by $B7C0 when the train is active. For the train the low and high source operands patch to $B75C and $B7DC.
Stage-indexed enable bits ORed into the immediate sprite mask at $816B during setup. The train path selects the row for index one.
Copy 256 colour lookup bytes from the stage source selected by $B1B9/$B1BE into $3000. For the temple, fill the entire working table with $0B instead.
Cached zero-based disk file number. A request for the selected asset set returns before changing the display or reading the disk.

Map the stage and subsection to a file number, skip a cached load, edit the filename digit, blank the display and call the packed serial loader. Restore raster IRQs and the game banking byte on return.
Mutable 16-byte filename template passed to KERNAL SETNAM. $B83B writes the file digit at $B87B before the serial read.
First 128 source glyphs of the title font, at eight bytes each. The page copy at $97EF places them at $0800, including the digits at glyphs $6C–$75 and start of the capitals.
Remaining 64 copied source glyphs. The title printer continues its capitals here from index $80 and uses a blank at $9C.
Source of title glyphs beginning at index $97, continuing the copied font beyond the $C000 address boundary.
Lower rows of the bank-3 screen selected at the raster split. Static cells draw the lettering and portraits, and updates at $8ABF replace the six score cells at $C351.
Eight 64-byte sprite patterns showing a bolt contracting into a thin line. The ranges start on each $40 boundary.
TIERTEX LIMITED text in the resident high-memory image. Its reader remains open.
Status panel character patterns $00–$7F, eight bytes each. The raster split's memory pointer selects these in VIC bank 3.
Status panel character patterns $80–$FF. The live icon slot beginning at $CF80 is updated by $9192.
Sprite sheet entries $40–$4F in bank 3, including Indy body outlines, bent arms and the upward-reaching pose. The player layer copier reads this bank with I/O hidden.
Sprite entries $50–$5F include walking, straight-legged and bent-legged outlines. Each entry uses 63 image bytes and one stride byte.
Sprite entries $60–$6F include player poses with horizontal arms and crouching silhouettes, followed by the first fill-mask entries.
Sprite entries $70–$7F contain solid player silhouette components paired with outline layers to give the character separately coloured fills.
Sprite entries $80–$8F include the mask layers for Indy's crouching and action poses.
Sprite entries $90–$9F continue the player fill shapes, then hold thin line shapes for the whip.
One 64-byte lower-body fill pattern. Its first 63 bytes matched the working pattern at $0AC0 in the caves snapshot.
The remaining sprite patterns on page $E4 continue the action fill layers. The following pages include bent-body masks and the thin whip-line animations from $E700.
Sprite entries $A0–$AF include the cross, shield, book, ring and torch motifs. The panel pointer table selects entries in this group directly in bank 3.
Sprite entries $B0–$BF include upright and bent human figure components in the shared bank.
Sprite entries $C0–$CF move from figure components to small projectile and line shapes.
The end of the narrow shape at $F200 leads into eight successive line shapes used by the shared graphics bank.
Sprite entries $D0–$DF include line and airborne shapes followed by upright character components.
This address in RAM lies two bytes into the sprite beginning at $F640. During disk reads, the KERNAL is visible here and $24C8 calls the ROM routine at this address instead.
